5.a: (1) Step one — the heatwave shifts supply leftward, so fewer mangoes are available at every price and the equilibrium price rises through a movement along the demand curve, (2) Step two — the higher price then induces a movement along the new supply curve, an expansion of quantity supplied, not a shift of the supply curve, (3) Step three — planting more trees is a long-run capacity response, a future rightward shift that belongs to a later season, since in the current market period supply is fixed by the harvest, (4) The error — the reporter treats a price-induced quantity change as a current supply shift that brings prices back down in the same period, the classic supply-response-to-price fallacy. A student who agrees with the reporter conflates short-run movements along the supply curve with long-run shifts of it.

2.a: (1) The fifty lakh apartment purchase — consumption, because housing services bought by a household are final consumption, not capital formation for the buyer, (2) The ten lakh crane — investment, because the builder's purchase of a capital good is capital formation, (3) The five lakh marble — imports, because spending on the foreign good leaks demand abroad, (4) Why the flat is not investment — in the national accounts only producer durables and inventory changes count as investment, so a household buying a house is not automatically investing. A wrong answer classifying the full fifty lakh as investment reveals the misconception that buying a house is always investment.

3.a: (1) The crude oil import — current account and a debit, because trade in goods records real resources, (2) The NRI deposit in an NRE account — capital account and a credit, because it raises India's financial liabilities to the rest of the world, (3) The World Bank grant — current account and a credit, because a grant is a current transfer, (4) The German factory purchase — capital account and a debit, because outward FDI acquires a foreign asset. A wrong classification such as treating the NRI deposit as a current-account item confuses financial flows with income and transfers, and wrong signs break the rule that inflow means credit and outflow means debit.

4.a: (1) Crude oil prices rise sharply — the import bill grows, demand for dollars shifts right, and the rupee depreciates, (2) US Fed hikes while RBI holds — higher US asset returns pull capital out, raising dollar demand while FPI selling cuts dollar supply, so both shifts push the exchange rate up and the rupee depreciates, (3) FPIs sell Indian stocks and repatriate — rupees are sold for dollars, raising dollar demand, so the demand curve shifts right and the rupee depreciates. A wrong answer such as a US rate hike making the dollar cheaper, or FPI selling increasing the supply of dollars, confuses asset returns with currency flows and misses who supplies what in the forex market.
